title: Giving without a receipt
hook: give, and let it go; don't keep score

segments.voice: Yesterday, the poor woman's lamp: one small flame, lit with a whole heart, still burning at dawn. Your line was small and wholehearted. What small thing did you give? Day one hundred thirty-seven, the end of the giving week.
screen: `THE POOR WOMAN'S LAMP — SMALL AND WHOLEHEARTED.`

segments.voice: Most of us keep a ledger we'd never admit to. I drove last time. I paid for dinner twice. I remembered her birthday; she forgot mine. It's not greed exactly. It's bookkeeping. And the ledger has a way of turning gifts into loans. You gave, but somewhere in the back office, it was written down, with a due date. This whole week has been about giving. It ends with the hardest part, the part that decides whether a gift stays a gift: what happens after you let go.
screen: `I DROVE LAST TIME.` → `THE LEDGER IN THE BACK OFFICE.` → `WHAT HAPPENS AFTER YOU LET GO.`

segments.voice: In one discourse, Sariputta asks the Buddha why the same gift can bear great fruit for one person and little for another. The Buddha answers with a ladder of motives. Someone gives hoping to get something back, or thinking I'll enjoy the reward of this later. That's a gift, and it bears some fruit. Higher up, someone gives simply because giving is good, or because it's the family custom, or to follow the example of wise people of old. And at the top, someone gives because it makes the mind calm and glad, as an ornament for the mind. Same rice, same bowl. What changes is what the giver is holding onto. A later Mahayana text, the Diamond Sutra, pushes it further. It says a bodhisattva should give without dwelling on anything: not on the gift, not on the receiver, not on the idea of being a giver. Give like a hand that opens and doesn't close again to check what it gave. Teachers sometimes call it giving that leaves no trace. The Pali word for that kind of generosity is caga, which also means letting go, relinquishing. Generosity and letting go are the same word. So look back at the week. Giving first opens the door. The bowl is open. Glad three times. Share the last bite. Attention is a gift. Small and wholehearted. And now, the last step: no receipt. Nobody's saying you can't notice who never pays. You can still be wise. But the gift itself, once it leaves your hand, is finished. It doesn't need a signature.
screen: `A LADDER OF MOTIVES.` · `AT THE TOP: AN ORNAMENT FOR THE MIND.` · `GIVE WITHOUT DWELLING ON ANYTHING.` · `CAGA: GENEROSITY IS LETTING GO.` · then, large: `NO RECEIPT.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one gift you're still keeping track of: a favor that wasn't returned, a kindness nobody noticed. Feel where the ledger sits in the body, maybe a tightness in the chest or jaw. Now, with the out-breath, imagine tearing up the receipt. Not because they deserved it, but because the gift was already complete. Breathe out again, and let the hand open. Rest in whatever lightness comes. The bell holds the time.
Giving without a receipt. Giving and letting go, with no score kept: the gift is complete the moment it leaves your hand.
Your line: no receipt. Today, give one thing anonymously: pay for a stranger's coffee, leave a note unsigned, fix something nobody will know you fixed. Day one hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Many Buddhists give anonymously or without expecting return, and in Mahayana traditions the perfection of giving is described as giving without clinging to the gift, the receiver or the self as giver.

giving as an ornament for the mind

myth: in the ladder of motives, giving to get something back bears no fruit at all
it bears some fruit; the fruit grows as the motive becomes freer.
the Pali word caga means both generosity and letting go
generosity and relinquishing are the same word.
giving without a receipt means you can never notice who takes advantage

fork.setup: Sariputta asks why the same gift bears great fruit for one person and little for another. what does the Buddha point to?
fork.reveal: he describes a ladder of motives, from hoping for a return up to giving as an ornament for the mind.

original.note: Pali: generosity, relinquishment; the same word for giving and for letting go.

trapdoor: what you thought: give, and hope they notice.
what it means: give and let go; the gift is complete when it leaves your hand.
what a scholar hears: AN 7.49 ranks motives for giving, the highest being to adorn the mind; the Diamond Sutra has the bodhisattva give without abiding in form.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 7.49 (Danamahapphala Sutta), motives for giving
Diamond Sutra (Vajracchedika Prajnaparamita), section 4, giving without dwelling

notes: The ladder of motives is condensed from AN 7.49 (it has seven steps, including 'I cook, they don't; it's not right not to give' and 'my good name will spread' in some readings); confirm the paraphrase.
The Diamond Sutra passage (section 4) is paraphrased; 'giving that leaves no trace' is a teaching phrase, not a quotation.
